Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Amadey and StealC Malware Network Disrupted, 27M Stolen Credentials Recovered
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Known Amadey/StealC binary execution or drop by SHA256 (DCU-extracted hashes) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Amadey/StealC disrupted C2 domain contact (Operation Endgame infrastructure) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Amadey/StealC disrupted C2 domain contact (Operation Endgame infrastructure) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host egress or DNS resolution to the specific Amadey and StealC command-and-control domains seized in the June 2026 Microsoft DCU / Operation Endgame disruption. Any internal host resolving or connecting to these confirmed-malicious C2 domains indicates an active or recently-active infostealer infection beaconing to its panel. Rationale: Uses the 12 exact C2 domains the article lists as the disrupted Amadey/StealC backbone; cross-checked against Microsoft DCU blog and Operation Endgame coverage (ESET, Bitsight, IBM X-Force) which confirm the same takedown, so these are second-source-corroborated malicious indicators, not single-article claims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/24/stealc-and-amadey-breaking-down-infostealers-and-the-cybercrime-services-that-deliver-them/ • https://securityaffairs.com/194173/cyber-crime/europol-disrupts-stealc-and-amadey-malware-infrastructure-in-operation-endgame.html • https://www.ibm.com/think/x-force/stealc-you-later-proofpoint-x-force-support-operation-endgame-disruptions
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Post-takedown sinkhole traffic: seized domains now resolve to law-enforcement/registrar sinkhole IPs, so a hit may reflect a sinkholed (already-neutralised) infection rather than live C2
  • Security researcher or TI-platform sandbox detonating Amadey/StealC samples inside the org's analysis VLAN
  • Threat-intel feed validation / DNS RPZ test harness deliberately querying known-bad domains
  • Passive DNS or scanning appliance (e.g. internal recursive resolver crawling) resolving the domain without an actual host infection
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-analysis","ti-lab"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath) making the connection; confirm it is not a sandbox/TI appliance. Pull the process tree and any binary hash on that host and check against UC2's StealC/Amadey hash list. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block all 12 C2 domains at the proxy/DNS firewall, and force-reset credentials for every account used on that device (infostealers harvest saved browser creds, cookies and VPN/SSO tokens) and revoke active session tokens. 3) Hunt: query SigninLogs/AADSignInEventsBeta for anomalous logins by that user (impossible travel, new device) indicating stolen-cookie reuse, and sweep all hosts for the same domains and hashes to scope additional infections.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["polse.us","roger99699.xyz","bluescry.com","secure.controlpanel.asia","neltron-geltron.shop","cdntestconnect.com","bartsen284.online","goodpanelforgoodjob.com","rebustan.top","svclsc.com","microsoft-telemetry.at","spasopro.at"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

 (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (c2Domains) | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=ClientIP, Indicator=Name, EventProduct="MicrosoftDNS", Src="DNS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Amadey/StealC binary execution or drop by SHA256 (DCU-extracted hashes) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or file-write of the specific Amadey loader and StealC infostealer binaries whose SHA256 hashes Microsoft DCU extracted from the disrupted samples. A match is a direct, high-confidence indicator that an analysed Amadey/StealC payload ran or was staged on the host. Rationale: Uses the 15 exact SHA256 hashes the article lists for Amadey/StealC binaries that DCU analysed and disrupted; these are sample-derived static IOCs whose match is unambiguous, and the campaign attribution is corroborated by the Microsoft DCU blog and Operation Endgame reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/24/stealc-and-amadey-breaking-down-infostealers-and-the-cybercrime-services-that-deliver-them/ • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/bitsight-aids-disruption-efforts-on-amadey-malware-and-stealc-malware
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis or reverse-engineering workstation where an analyst intentionally detonated a sample (the hash will match in a controlled VLAN)
  • EDR/AV detonation chamber or automated sandbox that pulls and executes submitted files
  • Threat-intel team copying the sample to an isolated host for triage without running it (file-write event only)
  • Backup/forensic image-mount surfacing a historical copy of the binary on a remediation host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("sandbox","re-vm","malware","detonation")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the EventKind (process exec vs file write) and the host's role — rule out sandbox/RE workstations. Capture the binary path, parent process and the user context; if a process exec, the infection is live. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file by hash across the fleet, kill the running process, and treat all credentials/cookies/tokens entered on that device as compromised — force password resets and revoke sessions (StealC harvests browser creds, wallets, VPN/SSO tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for child Amadey activity (additional dropped payloads) and outbound connections to the UC1 C2 domains, then sweep all endpoints for these 15 hashes to find sibling infections from the same loader campaign.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("polse.us", "roger99699.xyz", "bluescry.com", "secure.controlpanel.asia", "neltron-geltron.shop", "cdntestconnect.com", "bartsen284.online", "goodpanelforgoodjob.com", "rebustan.top", "svclsc.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["polse.us", "roger99699.xyz", "bluescry.com", "secure.controlpanel.asia", "neltron-geltron.shop", "cdntestconnect.com", "bartsen284.online", "goodpanelforgoodjob.com", "rebustan.top", "svclsc.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64","\Users\Public","\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64",
                              "\Users\Public", "\AppData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1027

            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'

falsepositives:

      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

SystemSettings.exe executing from non-standard path (SharkLoader DLL side-load host) AIInstallation High
Hunts the legitimate Windows binary SystemSettings.exe running from anywhere other than C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\ (or WinSxS). StrikeShark copies this signed binary to C:\ProgramData\, vendor-named decoy dirs (e.g. KasperskyLab), and %APPDATA%\xwreg / %APPDATA%\xgdf to side-load the malicious SystemSettings.dll (SharkLoader). The relocated binary is the launch point of the whole Cobalt Strike chain. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact relocation behaviour (copy SystemSettings.exe C:\ProgramData\, KasperskyLab/xwreg/xgdf decoy dirs). SystemSettings.exe only legitimately runs from ImmersiveControlPanel/WinSxS, making any other path near-deterministic for the side-load. Cross-checked against cybersecuritynews.com and cyberpress.org which confirm the SystemSettings.exe side-load and %APPDATA% working dirs. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin manually copying SystemSettings.exe to a test/staging folder during Settings-app troubleshooting
  • Backup/imaging software shadowing the binary into a snapshot path that lacks the WinSxS marker
  • Security-product self-protection sandboxes that copy and re-execute system binaries
  • Application-virtualization layers (App-V/MSIX) that surface SystemSettings.exe from a redirected path
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and FolderPath has @"\ccmcache\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath, SHA256, and parent of the relocated SystemSettings.exe; confirm a SystemSettings.dll exists in the SAME directory (legit copies never carry that DLL beside them) and check for DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat siblings. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and quarantine the directory; block the C2 domains (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com/.top, ms-tray.top) at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent (w3wp/java) for the originating webshell, and sweep the fleet for SystemSettings.exe in ProgramData/AppData plus the dual schtasks persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\" and FolderPath !has @"\WinSxS\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\SystemSettings.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\") and NewProcessName !has @"\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SystemSettings.exe Executed From Non-Standard Path (SharkLoader Side-Load)
id: 5f1c8a4e-3b2d-4c9a-9f6e-7a1b2c3d4e5f
status: experimental
description: Detects the legitimate Windows SystemSettings.exe running outside its canonical ImmersiveControlPanel/WinSxS location, used by StrikeShark to side-load SystemSettings.dll (SharkLoader).
references:
  - https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\SystemSettings.exe'
  filter_legit:
    Image|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Admin manually copying SystemSettings.exe for troubleshooting
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\SystemSettings.exe OR *\systemsettings.exe OR *\SYSTEMSETTINGS.EXE) -@Image:(*\ImmersiveControlPanel\* OR *\immersivecontrolpanel\* OR *\WinSxS\* OR *\winsxs\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\SystemSettings\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\(ImmersiveControlPanel|WinSxS)\\/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="SystemSettings.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT (like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\ImmersiveControlPanel\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\WinSxS\\%")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime lastTime dest user process_name process_path process parent_process_name count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="SystemSettings.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT (like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\ImmersiveControlPanel\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\WinSxS\\%")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime lastTime dest user process_name process_path process parent_process_name count
SharkLoader encrypted payload files dropped (DscCoreR.mui + SyncRes.dat + SystemSettings.dll) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of SharkLoader's distinctive component set in user-writable directories: the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll plus the encrypted in-memory-only modules DscCoreR.mui (Blowfish-decrypted) and SyncRes.dat (AES-128-decrypted API-hooking DLL). These filenames co-located in ProgramData/AppData are a near-unique campaign fingerprint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact module names DscCoreR.mui (Blowfish) and SyncRes.dat (AES-128) plus the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll — corroborated by cybersecuritynews.com describing the same DscCoreR.mui→SyncRes.dat decryption chain. DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat are non-Windows filenames so any user-writable occurrence is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party DSC (Desired State Configuration) tool legitimately staging a DscCore localized resource into ProgramData
  • Backup software re-hydrating an AppData folder that already contained the artifacts during a prior incident
  • Security-vendor sample-collection writing copies of these files into a quarantine/AppData path
  • Developer test fixtures that happen to reuse the SyncRes.dat name (rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","sensendr.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether all three components landed in one directory; hash SystemSettings.dll and check signing — SharkLoader's DLL is unsigned/forged. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the directory, and capture a memory image (SyncRes.dat/Beacon are decrypted only in memory). 3) Hunt: pivot to the SystemSettings.exe process that loads the DLL, the schtasks persistence, and outbound beacons to the campaign C2 domains; sweep fleet for the same filename triad.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("SystemSettings.dll","DscCoreR.mui","SyncRes.dat")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where not(FileName =~ "SystemSettings.dll" and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
| summarize Components=make_set(FileName), Paths=make_set(FolderPath), DistinctComponents=dcount(FileName), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("SystemSettings.dll","DscCoreR.mui","SyncRes.dat")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| summarize Components=make_set(TargetFileName), Paths=make_set(TargetFilePath), DistinctComponents=dcount(TargetFileName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: SharkLoader Encrypted Payload Files Written to User-Writable Path
id: 7c2e9b1a-4d5f-4a6b-8c3d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
status: experimental
description: Detects creation of SharkLoader's unique modules DscCoreR.mui and SyncRes.dat (and the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll) in ProgramData/AppData/Public.

Web server process spawning command shell to relocate SystemSettings.exe (post-webshell staging) AIExploitation High
Hunts internet-facing server processes (w3wp.exe for Exchange/SharePoint, java for Openfire) spawning a child that references SystemSettings.exe — the article's webshell-driven post-exploitation step where the attacker copies SystemSettings.exe out of ImmersiveControlPanel to stage the SharkLoader side-load. Rationale: Pairs the article's named initial-access surfaces (Exchange/SharePoint=w3wp, Openfire=java) with the exact webshell command observed (copy SystemSettings.exe / cd ImmersiveControlPanel). A web-server parent referencing SystemSettings.exe is not a benign pattern. Confirmed by cyberpress.org listing Exchange/SharePoint/Openfire as exploited entry points. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom in-house web app that legitimately shells out to launch the Windows Settings UI (uncommon on a server)
  • Server administrators invoking SystemSettings via a management web console
  • Application pool running a deployment script that references a like-named internal tool
  • SCOM/monitoring agents reading the Settings binary path via w3wp-hosted health checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and the w3wp/java application pool identity; pull recent IIS/Openfire access logs for the source IP and the requested webshell URL just before the spawn. 2) Contain: take the public-facing app offline or block the source IP, isolate the server, and preserve the webshell file and w3wp memory. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of that web server over 30 days, locate the dropped SystemSettings.exe/.dll, and check for the CVEs named in the article (ProxyLogon CVE-2021-26855, Openfire CVE-2023-32315, etc.) on the asset.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","tomcat9.exe","UMWorkerProcess.exe","MSExchangeFrontEndTransport.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688

| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharkLoader dropper masquerading as Cisco AnyConnect / Google Update installer AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the StrikeShark dropper executables that impersonate legitimate installers — GoogleUpdateStepup.exe, AutoUpdate.exe, and the AnyConnect predeploy lure — running from user-writable paths, and the decoy MSI written to %APPDATA%\reports\AnyConnect-win-4.msi while SharkLoader is dropped silently elsewhere in %APPDATA%. Rationale: Uses the article's exact dropper filenames (GoogleUpdateStepup.exe — a non-genuine Google name; AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9) and the %APPDATA%\reports\AnyConnect-win-4.msi decoy path. Corroborated by cybersecuritynews.com and cryptika.com which name the Cisco AnyConnect and Google Update lures. AutoUpdate.exe is generic, hence the user-writable-path constraint and Medium confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/ • https://www.cryptika.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures-to-drop-sharkloader-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party application updaters genuinely named AutoUpdate.exe running from AppData (Spotify-style updaters)
  • A user re-running a real Cisco Secure Client predeploy installer from their Downloads folder
  • Portable apps shipping their own updater binary in %APPDATA%
  • Software-packaging test labs staging installers under Temp
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "AutoUpdate.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropper and submit to VT/internal sandbox; check whether an MSI was written to %APPDATA%\reports\ and whether SharkLoader components (SystemSettings.dll/DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat) appeared in a sibling %APPDATA% dir within seconds. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the dropper and any dropped MSI/DLLs, and reset the user's credentials. 3) Hunt: trace delivery (email/download referrer via FileOriginUrl), and fleet-sweep for the dropper hashes and the GoogleUpdateStepup.exe/AnyConnect predeploy names.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("GoogleUpdateStepup.exe","AutoUpdate.exe")) or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)AnyConnect-win-4\.10\.04071-predeploy-k9"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith @"\GoogleUpdateStepup.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\AutoUpdate.exe" or CommandLine has "AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task persistence launching relocated SystemSettings.exe (SharkLoader) AIInstallation High
Hunts schtasks creation of a task whose action is the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe — SharkLoader's persistence, which the article/corroborators describe as a dual task set (one firing every 5 minutes for long-term persistence, one firing every second and self-deleting ~1.5s later for immediate launch). Rationale: Anchors on the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe being registered as a scheduled-task action — corroborated by cyberpress.org and cybersecuritynews.com, which document the dual 5-minute / 1-second self-deleting tasks executing the copied SystemSettings.exe from %APPDATA%\xwreg / xgdf. A scheduled task pointing at SystemSettings.exe is not a legitimate Windows pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A management tool scripting a Settings-related scheduled task (essentially never references the raw exe)
  • Admin recreating a task during troubleshooting that copies the binary path
  • MDM/RMM agents registering display/settings maintenance tasks
  • Imaging/provisioning runs that template scheduled tasks
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task XML (schtasks /query /xml or Event 4698) — confirm the action path points to a non-ImmersiveControlPanel SystemSettings.exe and note the trigger cadence (5-min or 1-sec). 2) Contain: delete both tasks, kill the SystemSettings.exe process tree, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: locate the side-load directory the task launches from, recover SharkLoader components, and fleet-sweep DeviceProcessEvents/Event 4698 for any scheduled task whose action references SystemSettings.exe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Created to Run SystemSettings.exe (SharkLoader Persistence)
id: 4d8f2a6c-5b3e-4c7d-9a1f-2b3c4d5e6f70
status: experimental
description: Detects schtasks /create whose action targets SystemSettings.exe, used by StrikeShark for SharkLoader persistence (5-minute and 1-second triggers).
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:*SystemSettings.exe* @CommandLine:*create*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*SystemSettings.exe*" Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process parent_process_name count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*SystemSettings.exe*" Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process parent_process_name count
SharkLoader / Cobalt Strike C2 egress to StrikeShark lookalike domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts connections or DNS to the StrikeShark C2 domains (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com, ms-record.top, ms-tray.top — Microsoft-lookalike infrastructure) and, behaviourally, the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe making outbound public connections from a non-Windows path (the Cobalt Strike beacon egress). Rationale: Uses the article's four C2 domains plus the corroborated behavioural anchor — a relocated SystemSettings.exe (the side-load/beacon host) making public egress. Note: the four domains are cited by the primary Kaspersky report; my second-source searches confirmed the SystemSettings.exe→Cobalt Strike beacon behaviour but did not independently re-list the domains, so the behavioural clause keeps the detection robust if the C2 rotates. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1574.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sandbox/malware-analysis VM detonating the sample and resolving the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IOC domains
  • Typosquat-monitoring services resolving the lookalike domains for brand protection
  • A proxy/DNS-sinkhole appliance logging the lookup as it blocks it (benign block)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process behind the connection/lookup (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) — if it's SystemSettings.exe from a non-Windows path, treat as confirmed beacon. 2) Contain: block all four domains and their resolved IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the host, and capture memory for the in-memory Cobalt Strike beacon. 3) Hunt: pivot the resolved IPs across DeviceNetworkEvents for other beaconing hosts, correlate to the SystemSettings.exe side-load and schtasks persistence, and check the C2 IP for the internet-wide scanning behaviour the article attributes to it.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:

    product: windows
detection:

    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Unified CM Flaw Exploited After PoC Reveals File-Write Path to Root

The Hacker News
2026-06-24 4 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors have begun to exploit a recently disclosed critical security flaw impacting Cisco Unified Communications Manager (Unified CM) and Unified Communications Manager Session Management Edition (Unified CM SME). The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-20230 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of improper input validation for specific HTTP requests that could allow an unauthenticated, remote

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF file:// file-write (CVE-2026-20230) exploitation attempt
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cisco Unified CM post-exploit JSP webshell drop under Apache Axis path (CVE-2026-20230)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF file:// file-write (CVE-2026-20230) exploitation attempt AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Cisco Unified CM WebDialer endpoint (/webdialer/) carrying a file:// scheme payload, the signature of CVE-2026-20230 SSRF abuse that writes arbitrary files to the appliance OS for root escalation. Article-specific because it pins both the WebDialer path and the file:// file-write payload class reported landing on exploitation decoys. Rationale: Uses two article-confirmed strings: the WebDialer endpoint directory (/webdialer/) and the file:// file-write payload class Defused observed on decoys; cross-checked against Cisco PSIRT advisory cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW, BleepingComputer, SOCRadar and Help Net Security. file:// in a /webdialer/ request is non-existent in legitimate click-to-call traffic, giving low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisco-unified-cm-sme-flaw-cve-2026-20230-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/24/cisco-unified-cm-flaw-exploited-to-drop-webshells-cve-2026-20230/ • https://x.com/DefusedCyber/status/2069074520057557244
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) firing CVE-2026-20230 plugins with file:// test payloads against /webdialer/
  • Internal red-team or pentest replaying the SSD/public PoC against the CUCM cluster
  • Security researchers validating the PoC from a known corporate jump host
  • Legitimate WebDialer click-to-call requests (these never contain a file:// scheme, so rarely collide)
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei", "Nmap", "masscan") and SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ip>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the target DestinationIP is a Unified CM/SME node with the Cisco WebDialer Web Service 'Started'; pull the full RequestURL and SourceIP, and check whether the source is a sanctioned scanner range or Tor exit node. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, block the SourceIP at the perimeter and disable the WebDialer Web Service (Serviceability > Control Center > Feature Services) per Cisco mitigation, then prioritise patching to 14SU6/15SU5. 3) HUNT: On the appliance review Tomcat webroot for newly written files, especially JSP under /_platform-services/axis2-web/, and pivot to UC #2 for webshell access from the same SourceIP.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/webdialer/" or DestinationServiceName has "webdialer"
| where RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file%3a%2f%2f", "file%3A%2F%2F")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Unified CM post-exploit JSP webshell drop under Apache Axis path (CVE-2026-20230) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts HTTP access to JSP files under the Cisco Unified CM Apache Axis directory (/_platform-services/axis2-web/), the second-stage webshell location attackers deploy after the WebDialer SSRF file-write to obtain command execution. Article/campaign-specific because the observed chain abuses the SSRF to plant a rogue Apache Axis service and write JSP webshells there. Rationale: Pivots on the campaign-specific second-stage path /_platform-services/axis2-web/ where the rogue Apache Axis JSP webshell is dropped (per Help Net Security / Defused reporting), distinct from UC #1's SSRF payload pivot. Medium confidence/FP because axis2-web ships some default JSPs (e.g. happyaxis.jsp), so pair with the same SourceIP seen in UC #1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/24/cisco-unified-cm-flaw-exploited-to-drop-webshells-cve-2026-20230/ • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisco-unified-cm-sme-flaw-cve-2026-20230-now-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate access to the default Apache Axis2 validation page (happyaxis.jsp / axis2-web/index.jsp) by an administrator
  • Cisco TAC or platform-services diagnostics touching /_platform-services/ during a support case
  • Vulnerability scanner crawling axis2-web JSP endpoints for the Axis2 admin console
  • Internal uptime/synthetic monitoring probing the axis2-web path
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL !has_any ("happyaxis.jsp", "/axis2-web/index.jsp") and RequestMethod in ("POST", "PUT")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the specific JSP filename and HTTP method/status in RequestURL; default Axis pages (happyaxis.jsp, index.jsp) returning 200 to internal monitoring are benign, an unfamiliar JSP name with POST bodies or query strings carrying commands is not. 2) CONTAIN: If the JSP is non-default, isolate the CUCM node from untrusted networks, capture the JSP file from the Tomcat webroot for forensics, and disable WebDialer; treat the host as compromised (patching alone does not evict an existing webshell). 3) HUNT: Correlate the SourceIP back to UC #1 file:// SSRF attempts, search for outbound connections / Tor traffic from the appliance, and review for added OS-level files or cron/service persistence consistent with root escalation.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/axis2-web/" or RequestURL has "/_platform-services/"
| where RequestURL has ".jsp"
| summarize Requests = count(), JspPaths = make_set(RequestURL, 20), Methods = make_set(RequestMethod, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName
| sort by LastSeen desc
