File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98") or SHA1 in~ ("2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98") or MD5 in~ ("2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98") or SHA1 in~ ("2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98") or MD5 in~ ("2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2758f4d71a2a2dfdefab81737c2d776b2a3dafe5844fdd2157e089a28447ca98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake AI Agent Skill Passed Security Scans and Reportedly Reached 26,000 Agents

The Hacker News
2026-06-23 7 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firm&nbsp;AIR&nbsp;built a fake AI agent skill, pushed it through a popular skill marketplace and an Instagram ad, and says it reached roughly 26,000 agents, including some on corporate accounts. Every skill security scanner the firm tested it against marked it safe. The payload was harmless by design: it collected the user's email address and did nothing else. The point was to show

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] On-disk 'brand-landingpage' fake AI agent skill artifact
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake AI Agent Skill Passed Security Scans and Reportedly Reached 26,000 Agents
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Agent download-and-run install of fake 'Stitch SDK' from stitch-design.ai
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AI agent skill phones home to lookalike Stitch domain stitch-design.ai · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
AI agent skill phones home to lookalike Stitch domain stitch-design.ai AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the AIR-controlled lookalike domain stitch-design.ai, which the fake 'brand-landingpage' skill instructs the agent to fetch its 'Stitch SDK' setup from. The legitimate Google Stitch tool lives at stitch.withgoogle.com, so any traffic to stitch-design.ai is the post-install external fetch a swapped page would weaponise. Rationale: stitch-design.ai is the explicit attacker-controlled lookalike named in the article (vs legit stitch.withgoogle.com); any resolution of it is the external fetch the skill points the agent at, with effectively zero benign reason to appear in enterprise DNS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.air.security/blog-posts/the-story-of-skills • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188840/how-a-malicious-ai-agent-skill-passed-security-checks-and-reached-26000-users.html • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-ai-agent-skill-passed-security.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually browsing stitch-design.ai during this very investigation
  • Threat-intel crawlers / URL-sandbox detonation resolving the domain from a security appliance
  • A passive-DNS or web-proxy prefetch service touching the domain
  • Researcher reproducing the AIR experiment in a lab tenant
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the InitiatingProcess that resolved/connected (node, python, claude, cursor, a shell) and pull that user's recently installed agent skills, looking for 'brand-landingpage' or any SKILL.md referencing stitch-design.ai. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block stitch-design.ai at proxy+DNS, and isolate the host if a child script was fetched and executed. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for download-and-run activity (UC2) and any data the agent could have exfiltrated; sweep all agent runtimes org-wide for the same domain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "stitch-design.ai" or RemoteUrl endswith "stitch-design.ai"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "stitch-design.ai"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f3a2c1e-9b44-4d77-bf2a-7c1e0a5d2f10
description: Detects DNS resolution of the AIR-controlled lookalike domain stitch-design.ai used by the fake brand-landingpage AI agent skill. Legitimate Google Stitch lives at stitch.withgoogle.com.

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*stitch-design.ai*" by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Agent download-and-run install of fake 'Stitch SDK' from stitch-design.ai AIInstallation High
Hunts the execution step of the brand-landingpage skill: a download/exec utility or AI-agent runtime invoked with stitch-design.ai in its command line, i.e. fetching and running the swapped 'Stitch SDK' install script. This is the foothold the article warns a real operator could use to read files or hit internal systems. Rationale: The article states the swapped page told the agent to 'download and run a script' from stitch-design.ai; a download/exec utility or agent runtime carrying that exact domain in its command line is the execution of that script and is unambiguously article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.air.security/blog-posts/the-story-of-skills • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188840/how-a-malicious-ai-agent-skill-passed-security-checks-and-reached-26000-users.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally testing the AIR demo skill in a sandbox
  • Security engineer reproducing the curl/wget fetch for analysis
  • Allowlist/proxy bypass tooling pre-fetching the URL for inspection
  • Red-team replay of the install chain during an authorised exercise
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full command line and the downloaded script path/hash (SHA256 in the result); determine whether the script actually executed and what it accessed. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the agent runtime process tree, block stitch-design.ai, and preserve the dropped script for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate everything the agent runtime could reach (mounted repos, cloud creds, internal APIs) and check for follow-on reads/exfil; sweep other developer hosts for the same skill.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "stitch-design.ai"
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","claude.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe","bash.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "stitch-design.ai"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

On-disk 'brand-landingpage' fake AI agent skill artifact AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the malicious skill package itself landing on developer/agent hosts: files or folders named brand-landingpage (the skill AIR shipped through a 36k-star marketplace repo). The article's first defender action is finding which skills are already installed, so this surfaces the artifact regardless of whether it has phoned out yet. Rationale: brand-landingpage is the exact, distinctive skill name AIR shipped; it is unlikely to collide with legitimate filenames and directly answers the article's 'find what is already running' guidance for the installed artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.air.security/blog-posts/the-story-of-skills • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188840/how-a-malicious-ai-agent-skill-passed-security-checks-and-reached-26000-users.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately building a brand landing page with a similarly-named local project folder
  • Generic marketing/web-dev repos that coincidentally use 'brand-landingpage' as a directory name
  • CI/build artifacts cloning the marketplace repo for inventory/scanning purposes
  • An internal skill-vetting pipeline pulling the sample for analysis
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (".claude\\skills", "\\skills\\", "agent", "\\.config\\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","git.exe","claude.exe","cursor.exe","code.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the discovered SKILL.md / skill manifest and confirm it references stitch-design.ai and a 'Stitch SDK' install step; verify provenance (was it merged from the 36k-star marketplace repo?). Step 2 (contain): Remove the skill from the agent's skill directory, pin/quarantine the marketplace source, and block stitch-design.ai. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate this host to UC1 (DNS) and UC2 (install exec) to determine if the skill already fetched the swapped payload; inventory all agent skills across the org and route new ones through a single controlled source.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "brand-landingpage" or FileName has "brand-landingpage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "brand-landingpage" or TargetFileName has "brand-landingpage"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

Malicious npm Packages Pose as PostCSS Tools to Deliver Windows RAT

The Hacker News
2026-06-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

npm install JS dropper writes settings.ps1 and executes it via PowerShell AIInstallation High
Hunts the install-time behaviour of the abdrizak PostCSS lookalike packages: a JavaScript dropper bundled in the package writes 'settings.ps1' to disk and launches it. Article-specific because it pins the exact stager filename spawned under a node.exe (npm) parent. Rationale: Pins the exact stager filename 'settings.ps1' (named in the article) under a node/npm parent — the install-time pivot is unique to this campaign and not covered by generic Office-spawns-script rules. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/lookalike-npm-package-postcss/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal npm package that ships a real settings.ps1 post-install script
  • Developer-authored PowerShell tooling coincidentally named settings.ps1 launched from a Node tooling wrapper
  • CI/CD runners executing project setup PowerShell from npm lifecycle hooks
  • Electron app updaters that shell out to PowerShell during install
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\node_modules\\@yourorg\\", "corp-setup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent node/npm command line; identify which npm package's lifecycle script spawned it and check npm/yarn logs for aes-decode-runner-pro, postcss-minify-selector(-parser). 2) Contain: isolate the dev host, kill the PowerShell/wscript tree, block nvidiadriver.net and 95.216.92.207 at egress. 3) Hunt: search the host for update.vbs, loader.py, *.pyd Nuitka modules and the HKCU Run key; rotate developer credentials (Chrome, git, npm, SSH) from the machine.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "settings.ps1"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "settings.ps1"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm Dropper Writes settings.ps1 Stager
id: 6f2a1c34-9b77-4e51-8c1d-2a4f0e9b7c10
description: Detects a PowerShell process executing settings.ps1 spawned from a Node/npm parent, matching the abdrizak PostCSS lookalike npm RAT dropper.
references:
  - https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/

logsource:

PostCSS RAT stager: curl.exe downloads payload from nvidiadriver[.]net AIDelivery High
Hunts the second-stage retrieval where settings.ps1 uses curl.exe to pull a ZIP payload from the driver-spoofing C2 domain nvidiadriver[.]net. Article-specific via the exact downloader binary plus the fake-driver domain. Rationale: Combines the named downloader (curl.exe) with the article's confirmed C2 domain nvidiadriver[.]net (corroborated by JFrog) — a high-fidelity ingress-tool-transfer pivot with near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/ • https://hackread.com/fake-npm-packages-postcss-tool-steal-chrome-password/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin manually testing connectivity to nvidiadriver.net during IR (expected once domain is known)
  • Security tooling/sandbox replaying the IOC for validation
  • A proxy or DNS sinkhole logging the domain as part of blocklist enforcement
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the curl command line and capture the full URL/ZIP name; check whether the download succeeded (file write of the ZIP, follow-on wscript.exe). 2) Contain: isolate host, block nvidiadriver.net at DNS/proxy and 95.216.92.207 at firewall, kill the script chain. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts contacting nvidiadriver.net, search for the extracted update.vbs/loader.py and the HKCU Run persistence; rotate dev credentials.

| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "nvidiadriver.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "nvidiadriver.net"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

update.vbs extracted from ZIP and launched via wscript.exe AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the 'update.vbs' VBScript (unpacked from the downloaded ZIP) by wscript.exe, which sets up the bundled Python runtime and launches loader.py. Article-specific through the exact script name and interpreter. Rationale: Targets the exact VBScript name 'update.vbs' run under wscript/cscript named in the article — a distinct execution-stage pivot from the earlier PowerShell/curl stages. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/ • https://www.cryptika.com/windows-rat-uses-encrypted-http-c2-and-registry-persistence-after-npm-infection/

  • Vendor application installers that bootstrap a runtime via VBScript

PostCSS RAT C2 beacon to 95.216.92[.]207 on port 8080 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound RAT command-and-control to the hardcoded server 95.216.92[.]207:8080 used by the Nuitka-compiled Python RAT (api.pyd HTTP C2). Article-specific via the exact IP:port. Rationale: Uses the article's exact C2 endpoint 95.216.92[.]207:8080 (confirmed by JFrog) — an IP+port match is a low-FP, high-confidence alerting signal independent of host-side process telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/ • https://www.cryptika.com/windows-rat-uses-encrypted-http-c2-and-registry-persistence-after-npm-infection/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/threat-intel validation traffic to the known-bad IP after publication
  • A security scanner probing the IOC range
  • Sinkhole or honeypot infrastructure logging the connection
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect python.exe from a bundled runtime); confirm whether the beacon is recurring. 2) Contain: block 95.216.92.207 at the firewall, isolate the host, kill the python/wscript tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process to find update.vbs/loader.py/*.pyd, the HKCU Run key, and Chrome credential-store access; check all hosts for the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "95.216.92.207" and RemotePort == 8080
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "95.216.92.207" and DestinationPort == 8080
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PostCSS RAT Registry Run-key persistence under HKCU CurrentVersion\Run AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the RAT's persistence: a value written to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run that re-launches the wscript/update.vbs or bundled python loader at logon. Persistence detail confirmed by JFrog research. Rationale: Targets the JFrog-confirmed HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run persistence pointing at the wscript/update.vbs/python loader chain — a distinct persistence pivot from the execution and C2 UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/ • https://www.cryptika.com/windows-rat-uses-encrypted-http-c2-and-registry-persistence-after-npm-infection/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate apps that register a python or wscript-based updater in the Run key
  • Developer tooling auto-start entries referencing python scripts
  • Vendor agents that persist a VBScript launcher at logon
  • User-installed utilities that auto-start a .py helper
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full RegistryValueData and the writing process; determine whether the path resolves to a user-temp/AppData location (suspicious) vs Program Files (likely benign). 2) Contain: remove the Run value, isolate host, kill the persisted process. 3) Hunt: correlate with update.vbs execution, the Nuitka *.pyd modules, and C2 to 95.216.92.207:8080; sweep the fleet for the same value-data patterns.

title: PostCSS npm RAT Run-Key Persistence (wscript/python)

description: Detects a Run-key value pointing to update.vbs, wscript, or a python loader, matching the persistence used by the PostCSS npm-delivered RAT.
references:
  - https://research.jfrog.com/post/from-postcss-typosquat-to-windows-rat/
  - https://www.cryptika.com/windows-rat-uses-encrypted-http-c2-and-registry-persistence-after-npm-infection/

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentVersion\Run\* OR *\currentversion\run\*) @Details:(*update.vbs* OR *wscript* OR *loader.py* OR *\python*)

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentVersion\\Run*" AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*update.vbs*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*wscript*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*loader.py*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\python*") by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
@withgoogle/stitch-sdk developer-credential exfil to stitch-production[.]org AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the parallel npm/dev-credential-stealer campaign: the @withgoogle/stitch-sdk package harvests developer secrets (Claude Code, git config, ~/.git-credentials, SSH keys, GitHub CLI, npm config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json) and exfiltrates to stitch-production[.]org/api/v1. Article-specific via the exact exfil domain. Rationale: Uses the exact exfil domain stitch-production[.]org named in the article for the @withgoogle/stitch-sdk credential stealer — covers the article's required credential_access/exfil phase with a high-fidelity domain IOC. sentinel_kql uses DnsEvents.Name (the valid queried-domain column) after the prior IPAddresses schema error was removed. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-npm-packages-pose-as-postcss.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate access to a real 'stitch' product on a similarly named domain (verify exact FQDN)
  • Threat-intel/IR validation lookups of the IOC domain after publication
  • DNS sinkhole or blocklist enforcement logging the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the process resolving/connecting to stitch-production.org; confirm @withgoogle/stitch-sdk in npm/yarn lockfiles. 2) Contain: block the domain at DNS/proxy, isolate the developer host. 3) Hunt: assume all eight credential sources (Claude Code, git config, ~/.git-credentials, SSH keys, GitHub CLI, npm config, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json) are compromised — rotate every one of them and audit recent git/npm/docker/registry activity from the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "stitch-production.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "stitch-production.org"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-11645")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-11645")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

WhatsApp VBScript Campaign Uses Fake Documents to Install ManageEngine RMM Tool

The Hacker News
2026-06-23 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Direct messages sent via WhatsApp are being used to distribute malicious Visual Basic Script (VBScript) files that lead to the installation of legitimate Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) software. Per findings from Kaspersky, the active campaign is targeting users of WhatsApp Desktop and WhatsApp Web across Malaysia, Brazil, India, Mexico, Singapore, the U.K., Spain, Taiwan, Australia,

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Financial-lure .vbs written into WhatsApp Desktop session folder
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WhatsApp Desktop (WhatsApp.Root.exe) spawning WScript/CScript · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — WhatsApp VBScript Campaign Uses Fake Documents to Install ManageEngine RMM Tool
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] UAC bypass via ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin set to 0 by script host · [LLM] ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMSAgent.msi) silent install as RMM implant · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] WScript/CScript C2 egress to WhatsApp-campaign download infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
WhatsApp Desktop (WhatsApp.Root.exe) spawning WScript/CScript AIExploitation High
Hunts the WhatsApp VBScript campaign's entry point on WhatsApp Desktop, where the client background process WhatsApp.Root.exe directly spawns wscript.exe/cscript.exe to run an attached .vbs lure. A messaging client launching the Windows Script Host is anomalous and article-specific. Rationale: WhatsApp.Root.exe -> wscript.exe/cscript.exe is the exact parent-child chain Kaspersky documented for WhatsApp Desktop infections; a chat client launching WSH essentially never happens benignly, making this near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/whatsapp-phishing-attack-uses-fake-business-docs-to-hack-pcs/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user/admin saving a legitimate .vbs received in WhatsApp and double-clicking it for genuine business automation
  • Security testing / red-team replaying WSH lures from a chat client
  • EDR telemetry mislabeling a shared parent PID during rapid process churn
  • Helpdesk-distributed VBS maintenance scripts shared over WhatsApp in small businesses
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\Program Files\\","\\Windows\\System32\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the spawned wscript ProcessCommandLine and the dropped .vbs path (expect AppData\Local\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions); read the script for obfuscation and download URLs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript process tree, and quarantine the .vbs. 3) Hunt: check the same host for outbound connections to 202.61.160.0/24 or *.aliyuncs.com download attempts, the ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0 registry change, and any UEMSAgent.msi / ManageEngine Endpoint Central install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WScript/CScript C2 egress to WhatsApp-campaign download infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the malicious VBScript reaching out to the campaign's second-stage servers to pull additional payloads and the ManageEngine ZIP. Pivots on the corroborated C2 IP block and download domains, scoped to script-host or browser-driven egress. Rationale: The 202.61.160.0/24 cluster plus 38.55.151.63 and the baskwms/msopsa/shoppes/baoxis/aliyuncs download hosts are explicit IOCs in Securelist; the .201 node is the one cross-linked to ValleyRAT/Gh0st infrastructure, so any contact is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or analyst VM deliberately detonating the sample
  • Shared OSS/CDN ranges (Alibaba aliyuncs) hosting benign content for other apps
  • Security scanner / proxy pre-fetching the URLs for inspection
  • IOC re-use where an IP is reassigned to a benign tenant after takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which process initiated the connection (expect wscript/cscript or msiexec) and whether a file was retrieved. 2) Contain: block the IP set and domains at the firewall/proxy and isolate any host with a successful connection. 3) Hunt: enumerate all org hosts that resolved the download domains, then check those endpoints for the WhatsApp.Root->wscript chain and ManageEngine Endpoint Central install.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msiexec.exe") or isnotempty(RemoteUrl))
| where RemoteIP in ("202.61.160.201","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.208","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63")
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("baskwms.top","msopsa.top","shoppes.help","baoxis.cc","baolongwes.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2 = dynamic(["202.61.160.201","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.208","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (C2)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAC bypass via ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin set to 0 by script host AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's second-stage VBScript disabling the UAC admin consent prompt by setting HKLM Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 0, scoped to a script-host initiator to keep it tight. Rationale: Securelist names the exact registry value (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin -> 0); pairing the value with a script-host/LOLBin initiator separates the campaign from rare legitimate group-policy hardening. Falcon FDR has no generic registry-value event for non-ASEP keys, so falcon_logscale_query is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
ATT&CKT1548.002 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GPO / Intune baseline lowering UAC on kiosk or lab machines
  • Sysadmin temporarily disabling UAC during software packaging
  • Imaging/build automation (MDT/SCCM task sequence) that sets UAC policy
  • Developer disabling UAC prompts on a personal dev box
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe","TiWorker.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process and command line — campaign sets the value from wscript/cscript, not from a GPO or trusted installer. 2) Contain: revert ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 1, isolate the host, and capture the parent script. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for the WhatsApp.Root->wscript chain, C2 egress to 202.61.160.0/24, and a subsequent UEMSAgent.msi install indicating RMM deployment.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Policies\System"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin"
| where RegistryValueData in ("0","0x0","0x00000000")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryValue =~ "ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin"
| where RegistryValueData in ("0","0x0","0x00000000","DWORD (0x00000000)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMSAgent.msi) silent install as RMM implant AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's terminal objective: silent installation of ManageEngine Endpoint Central via msiexec deploying UEMSAgent.msi, which grants the actor persistent remote access. Pivots on the specific package name and script-driven, silent msiexec invocation. Rationale: Securelist enumerates the exact stage-3 package contents (UEMSAgent.msi/.mst, DCAgentServerInfo.json, setup1.vbs); msiexec carrying 'UEMSAgent' under a script-host parent is the deployment of the RMM implant rather than a normal admin push. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1219 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organizations that legitimately deploy ManageEngine Endpoint Central agents via SCCM/Intune
  • IT re-imaging or re-enrolling endpoints into a sanctioned UEMS server
  • MSP-managed fleets where the RMM agent install is routine
  • Software inventory tools re-running the MSI to repair the agent
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent of msiexec (campaign uses wscript/setup1.vbs, not a management agent) and read DCAgentServerInfo.json to identify the configured server — compare against your sanctioned UEMS server. 2) Contain: if the server is unknown, isolate the host, stop/uninstall the rogue UEMSAgent, and block the configured server. 3) Hunt: pivot on the configured server IP across the fleet and review for prior UAC tampering and 202.61.160.0/24 C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "UEMSAgent" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DCAgentServerInfo","UEMSAgent.mst")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "UEMSAgent"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ManageEngine UEMSAgent Silent Install via Msiexec
id: c3a1e8f6-4d22-4b90-91a7-5e6f2b9c1d83
description: Detects msiexec installing the ManageEngine Endpoint Central UEMSAgent package used as an RMM implant in the WhatsApp VBScript campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1218.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\msiexec.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'UEMSAgent'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\msiexec.exe OR *\MsiExec.exe OR *\MSIEXEC.EXE) @CommandLine:(*UEMSAgent* OR *uemsagent*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/msiexec\.exe$/i
| regex("UEMSAgent", field=CommandLine, flags=i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="msiexec.exe" AND Processes.process="*UEMSAgent*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="msiexec.exe" AND Processes.process="*UEMSAgent*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Financial-lure .vbs written into WhatsApp Desktop session folder AIDelivery Medium
Catches the delivery stage before execution: a .vbs file (often a financial/business-themed lure name) created inside the WhatsApp Desktop package/Sessions directory. Targets the specific drop location and lure naming Kaspersky observed. Rationale: Kaspersky gives both the exact drop path (AppData\Local\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions) and concrete financial lure filenames; a .vbs landing in the WhatsApp package directory is abnormal and provides pre-execution warning. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://www.technadu.com/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-installs-manageengine-rmm-kaspersky-warns/629801/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately saving a non-malicious .vbs received over WhatsApp into the cache folder
  • Backup/sync tooling copying WhatsApp media+attachment folders
  • Security tooling staging a sample in the same path during analysis
  • Benign automation scripts a user habitually shares with contacts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("WhatsApp.exe","WhatsApp.Root.exe","WhatsAppDesktop.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped .vbs and check for obfuscation, Chinese 'Windows Update' decoy comments, and embedded download URLs; correlate with whether wscript later executed it. 2) Contain: quarantine the file; if executed, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 / lure filenames and for WhatsApp.Root->wscript executions to find recipients who clicked.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".vbs"
| where FolderPath has_any ("5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm","WhatsAppDesktop")
    or FileName in~ ("Financial Reports.vbs","Account Statement.vbs","Debt confirmation.vbs","Statement of Debt(30K).vbs","Outstanding Payment List.vbs","Extrato de Conciliação.vbs","Penyata bank.vbs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".vbs"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm","WhatsAppDesktop")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VBScript Lure Dropped in WhatsApp Desktop Folder
id: a7d2c910-6e34-4b81-8f25-3c9a1b4d6e72
description: Detects creation of a .vbs file inside the WhatsApp Desktop package/Sessions directory, the delivery stage of the WhatsApp VBScript ManageEngine RMM campaign.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*WhatsAppDesktop*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-11645")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-11645")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-11645")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-11645")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"

SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Klue/Icarus: bulk Salesforce CRM record retrieval via connected app (Case/Contact/Account/Opportunity) · [LLM] Salesforce API access bearing python-requests/aiohttp automation user-agent (Icarus OAuth abuse) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Klue/Icarus: bulk Salesforce CRM record retrieval via connected app (Case/Contact/Account/Opportunity) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the high-volume automated read/export of Salesforce CRM objects performed by the compromised Klue OAuth integration during the June 2026 Icarus/UNC6395 campaign. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact CRM objects (Case, Contact, Account, Opportunity) that were mass-queried via SOQL/bulk export by an authorized third-party connected app rather than an interactive user. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CRM objects (Case/Contact/Account/Opportunity) that Mandiant/Google Cloud confirmed were bulk-SOQL-queried and exported by the abused OAuth connected app, plus a per-hour volume threshold that separates a productized SaaS connector's steady sync from an attacker's automated mass extraction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4187907/klue-breach-exposed-salesforce-crm-data-through-stolen-oauth-tokens.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftthreatprotectionblog/protect-against-oauth-attacks-in-salesforce-with-microsoft-defender/4450584
ATT&CKT1119 T1213 T1567.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Nightly/scheduled Klue competitive-intel sync legitimately reading Account/Opportunity records
  • Sales-ops bulk report exports or Salesforce Data Loader jobs run by admins
  • Data-warehouse ETL connectors (Fivetran, Informatica, Mulesoft) extracting CRM objects on a schedule
  • SaaS backup tooling (OwnBackup/Own, Spanning) performing full-object snapshots
  • Marketing/RevOps enrichment integrations doing periodic full-table pulls
Suppression filter
| where AccountObjectId !in ("<known-klue-integration-objectid-AFTER-revalidation>") and not (UserAgents has_any ("Salesforce Data Loader","OwnBackup","Fivetran","Informatica"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the AccountObjectId/CONNECTED_APP_NAME driving the spike — confirm whether it is the Klue integration service account and compare the hour's RecordOps to the prior 30-day baseline for that identity. Pull the UserAgents and SrcIPs aggregated. 2) CONTAIN: If it is Klue (or any unexpected connected app) exceeding baseline, disable/revoke the connected app's OAuth authorization in Salesforce Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage and revoke its tokens; do not just block the IP. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same AccountObjectId across all Salesforce ActionTypes for the last 14 days, look for python-requests/aiohttp user-agents (UC2) and first-seen source ISPs (UC3), and enumerate exactly which records were read for breach-notification scoping.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","ReportExport","Report exported","Bulk","Mass","Export","Read")
| where ObjectType in~ ("Case","Contact","Account","Opportunity") or isempty(ObjectType)
| summarize RecordOps = count(),
            DistinctRecords = dcount(ObjectId),
            ObjectsTouched = make_set(ObjectType, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 8)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where RecordOps > 1000   // bulk automated pull; productized Klue sync runs far lower, attacker mass-export spikes
| order by RecordOps desc

sourcetype="sfdc:reportexport" OR sourcetype="sfdc:api" OR sourcetype="sfdc:restapi" OR sourcetype="sfdc:bulkapi"
| eval crm_object=coalesce(ENTITY_NAME, ENTITY)
| where (crm_object IN ("Case","Contact","Account","Opportunity")) OR (EVENT_TYPE IN ("ReportExport","BulkApi","BulkApiV2"))

| where RecordOps > 1000
| sort - RecordOps
Salesforce API access bearing python-requests/aiohttp automation user-agent (Icarus OAuth abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Salesforce API/bulk calls whose user-agent is a raw Python HTTP library (python-requests, aiohttp), which Mandiant attributed to the Icarus/UNC6395 exfiltration scripts in the Klue/Salesloft-Drift OAuth campaign. Article-specific because a productized SaaS connector like Klue does not present python-requests/aiohttp as its session user-agent — that fingerprint indicates the stolen token is being driven by an attacker's ad-hoc script. Rationale: The python-requests/aiohttp user-agent is a high-fidelity, second-source-confirmed (Mandiant/Google Cloud) fingerprint of the Icarus exfil scripts driving a stolen OAuth token, and it cleanly distinguishes scripted attacker access from a legitimate productized connector's normal session UA. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.rescana.com/post/salesloft-drift-oauth-token-breach-enables-salesforce-data-theft-in-unc6395-icarus-attack-campaign-august-2026
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004 T1071.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-house Python integration scripts legitimately calling the Salesforce REST/Bulk API with a default user-agent
  • CI/CD jobs or scheduled data pipelines built on requests/aiohttp pulling CRM data
  • QA/sandbox automation against a production org
  • A developer running an ad-hoc simple_salesforce/requests script for a one-off pull
  • Low-code/iPaaS connector that happens to surface a python-requests UA
Suppression filter
| where AccountObjectId !in ("<known-internal-python-integration-objectid>") and AccountType != "DeveloperSandbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine which AccountObjectId/CONNECTED_APP the python-requests/aiohttp sessions authenticated as — if it is an OAuth connected-app/service identity (not a named developer), treat as high priority and pull the SrcIPs and Objects accessed. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the connected app's OAuth tokens and disable the integration in Salesforce; rotate the integration credential/secret. 3) HUNT: Correlate the same SrcIPs/AccountObjectId against UC1 (bulk record volume) and UC3 (new source infra); if confirmed, enumerate every object/record touched by those sessions for notification scope and check for log-tampering (Setup Audit Trail gaps).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","aiohttp","python-urllib","Python/3")
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 12),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 12),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 8),
            AnonProxy = make_set(IsAnonymousProxy, 3)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, UserAgent
| order by EventCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 12),

            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 8),
            AnonProxy = make_set(IsAnonymousProxy, 3)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, UserAgent
| order by EventCount desc

sourcetype="sfdc:api" OR sourcetype="sfdc:restapi" OR sourcetype="sfdc:bulkapi" OR sourcetype="sfdc:reportexport"
| where like(lower(USER_AGENT),"%python-requests%") OR like(lower(USER_AGENT),"%aiohttp%") OR like(lower(USER_AGENT),"%python-urllib%")
